idea: Natural selection requires heritable variation associated with differences in survival or reproduction in a particular environment. Populations change across generations as contributions to the next generation differ. Individuals can acclimate, but an individual’s need does not directly generate the specific inherited variation that solves it.
formula: Heritable variation + differential reproduction → population change
steps: A population includes two heritable color variants before a habitat change.
Predators capture one variant more frequently under the new conditions.
If survivors contribute unequally to offspring, color-associated allele frequencies can change.
The habitat filtered preexisting variation rather than instructing every organism to mutate toward the favored color.
trap: Individuals do not evolve a population’s allele frequency during their own lifetime.
challenge: Why must a favored trait be heritable for selection on that trait to produce a lasting inherited shift?
solution: Offspring must tend to inherit the relevant variation. A purely noninherited difference can affect individual survival without being transmitted as that trait.

questions.prompt: Which condition is necessary for natural selection on an inherited trait?
options: A conscious decision by every organism.
Identical genotypes and identical reproductive success.
A guarantee that every mutation is beneficial.
Trait-associated differences in reproductive contribution.
questions.explain: Trait-associated differences in reproductive contribution.
questions.hint: Individuals do not evolve a population’s allele frequency during their own lifetime.

questions.prompt: A population becomes more resistant after exposure. Which explanation is consistent with selection?
options: Each individual changes every allele because it needs to.
All allele frequencies must remain unchanged.
Heritable resistant variants contribute more offspring under exposure.
Exposure directs every mutation to the same useful sequence.
questions.explain: Heritable resistant variants contribute more offspring under exposure.
questions.hint: Individuals do not evolve a population’s allele frequency during their own lifetime.

title: Analyze fitness as a relative reproductive outcome
goal: Analyze fitness as a relative reproductive outcome. Practice: interpret selection data.
idea: Fitness is evaluated relative to reproductive contribution in a specified environment. Different selection patterns can favor one extreme, both extremes or intermediate phenotypes. A trait beneficial in one environment can be disadvantageous in another; adaptation is not a universal march toward perfection.
formula: Compare reproductive contributions under specified conditions
steps: Two genotypes begin at the same abundance.
Under treatment, one produces on average two viable descendants and the other one.
Relative contribution favors the first in that setting.
Change the environment and measure again before claiming it is always the fitter genotype.
trap: Survival matters through its effects on reproduction; long life alone does not guarantee higher evolutionary fitness.
challenge: Explain how a trade-off can maintain variation when no genotype is best in every situation.
solution: Different conditions or life-history costs can favor different variants, preventing one from having an advantage across all contexts.

questions.prompt: Which measurement most directly estimates fitness in a simple model?
options: The number of mutations regardless of effects.
How complex an organism looks.
Relative contribution of viable offspring to later generations.
Body size alone in every species.
questions.explain: Relative contribution of viable offspring to later generations.
questions.hint: Survival matters through its effects on reproduction; long life alone does not guarantee higher evolutionary fitness.

questions.prompt: Selection favoring intermediate values is called…
options: A universal increase in mutation rate.
Stabilizing selection.
Directional selection toward one extreme by definition.
Random genetic drift by definition.
questions.explain: Stabilizing selection.
questions.hint: Survival matters through its effects on reproduction; long life alone does not guarantee higher evolutionary fitness.

title: Distinguish human selection from directed mutation
goal: Distinguish human selection from directed mutation. Practice: design an evolutionary comparison.
idea: Artificial selection occurs when humans preferentially breed organisms with desired heritable traits. It changes reproductive contributions through a chosen criterion. It can shift trait distributions but can also increase inbreeding or correlated undesirable traits. The breeder’s intention does not make mutations occur exactly as needed.
formula: Human choice changes which inherited variants reproduce
steps: A breeder chooses plants with larger seeds from each generation.
If seed-size variation has a heritable component, the offspring distribution can shift.
Compare with randomly chosen parents under matched growing conditions.
A difference supports response to selection, while shared environments and correlated traits still require attention.
trap: Artificial selection changes reproduction; it is not the same process as editing a specific DNA sequence.
challenge: Why might selecting a trait fail to change it strongly over generations?
solution: Much observed variation might be environmental, or genetic constraints and trade-offs may limit response.

questions.prompt: What makes selection artificial?
options: Every offspring is genetically identical.
Humans choose breeding contributions according to desired traits.
Mutations become perfectly predictable.
Inheritance no longer operates.
questions.explain: Humans choose breeding contributions according to desired traits.
questions.hint: Artificial selection changes reproduction; it is not the same process as editing a specific DNA sequence.

questions.prompt: What is a useful control for a breeding-selection experiment?
options: A comparable population with random parent choice.
A different species in an unrelated habitat only.
The largest selected offspring alone.
A photograph without measurements.
questions.explain: A comparable population with random parent choice.
questions.hint: Artificial selection changes reproduction; it is not the same process as editing a specific DNA sequence.

title: Calculate allele frequencies and identify evolutionary forces
goal: Calculate allele frequencies and identify evolutionary forces. Practice: calculate allele frequency.
idea: Population genetics tracks alleles across generations. Selection, mutation, migration and random sampling can alter frequencies. Genetic drift can be especially strong in small populations and is not directed toward adaptive outcomes. Gene flow moves alleles among populations through successful migrants or gametes.
steps: In 50 diploid individuals, count 20 AA,20 Aa and10 aa.
There are 100 gene copies at this locus.
A copies number 2×20+20=60, so p=0.60.
This calculation does not require assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.
trap: An allele frequency can be calculated from counts without inferring that genotype frequencies are at equilibrium.
challenge: A storm leaves a small random set of survivors. Explain why an allele-frequency shift need not be adaptive.
solution: Chance survival can sample alleles unevenly even when the allele had no effect on storm survival. That is drift, with possible bottleneck effects.

questions.prompt: Among 100 diploid individuals, 40 are AA,40 Aa,20 aa. What is p(A)?
questions.hint: Count A copies and divide by 200.

questions.prompt: What is gene flow?
options: Only a new mutation in one isolated individual.
Translation within one cell.
A guaranteed loss of every rare allele.
Movement of alleles between populations through successful reproduction.
questions.explain: Movement of alleles between populations through successful reproduction.
questions.hint: An allele frequency can be calculated from counts without inferring that genotype frequencies are at equilibrium.

title: Use Hardy–Weinberg as a null model
goal: Use Hardy–Weinberg as a null model. Practice: use a population null model.
idea: For a diploid two-allele locus, random mating predicts genotype frequencies p²,2pq,q² when its model assumptions apply. Stable allele frequencies additionally require no selection, migration or mutation and a sufficiently large population to neglect drift. Deviation can motivate further investigation without identifying a unique cause.
formula: p+q=1; p²+2pq+q²=1
steps: Suppose q=0.2 for allele a in a population meeting the stated model.
Then p=0.8.
Expected genotype frequencies are AA=0.64,Aa=0.32,aa=0.04.
In 200 individuals, expected counts are128,64,8; actual random samples can differ.
trap: Dominant-phenotype frequency is not p. Inferring q from a recessive phenotype requires model assumptions and the correct phenotype mapping.
challenge: Under the model, recessive phenotype frequency is0.09 with complete dominance. Find q,p and expected heterozygote frequency.
solution: q=√0.09=0.3,p=0.7,so2pq=0.42. These are model-dependent inferences.

questions.prompt: For p=0.7 and q=0.3 under Hardy–Weinberg, what is expected heterozygote frequency?
questions.hint: Use2pq.

questions.prompt: A sample differs from Hardy–Weinberg expectations. What follows?
options: Every gene has mutated.
The sample automatically establishes a new species.
Several biological or sampling explanations may need testing.
Selection is proven as the only possible cause.
questions.explain: Several biological or sampling explanations may need testing.
questions.hint: Dominant-phenotype frequency is not p. Inferring q from a recessive phenotype requires model assumptions and the correct phenotype mapping.

title: Compare independent lines of evolutionary evidence
goal: Compare independent lines of evolutionary evidence. Practice: evaluate evolutionary evidence.
idea: Fossils, molecular sequences, biogeography and homologous structures can support evolutionary relationships. Evidence is strongest when independent observations agree with a testable ancestry model. Similar function alone can reflect convergence, so function and ancestry must be distinguished. Fossil records are informative despite incomplete sampling.
formula: Converging evidence strengthens an ancestry inference
steps: Two lineages share a detailed anatomical pattern and several sequence similarities.
Compare these features with outgroups and alternative relationships.
Agreement across independent features supports a proposed shared ancestry.
A similar streamlined shape alone might instead reflect similar environmental selection.
trap: A missing fossil for one interval does not imply that all other evolutionary evidence disappears.
challenge: Contrast homologous and analogous traits.
solution: Homologous traits derive from a shared ancestral feature; analogous similarities can arise independently through convergence. Shared function alone does not settle the distinction.

questions.prompt: What most strengthens a proposed relationship?
options: Only similar size.
Ignoring contradictory observations.
Concordant molecular, anatomical and historical evidence.
Only similar habitat use.
questions.explain: Concordant molecular, anatomical and historical evidence.
questions.hint: A missing fossil for one interval does not imply that all other evolutionary evidence disappears.

questions.prompt: Which similarity can arise by convergent evolution?
options: An individual’s unchanged genotype between measurements.
A similar functional shape evolving independently in different lineages.
Only a shared nucleotide inherited from a recent ancestor.
Every chromosome in two clones.
questions.explain: A similar functional shape evolving independently in different lineages.
questions.hint: A missing fossil for one interval does not imply that all other evolutionary evidence disappears.

title: Explain common ancestry without ranking living species
goal: Explain common ancestry without ranking living species. Practice: explain common ancestry.
idea: Shared molecular machinery and inherited features support common ancestry. Modern lineages have all continued evolving since divergence. A living species placed near another on a tree is not automatically its direct ancestor, and common ancestry does not mean organisms are identical in all traits.
formula: Shared descent can explain nested similarities
steps: Compare a conserved molecular system across several lineages.
Shared detailed features can be inherited from an ancestral system.
New lineage-specific changes accumulate after divergence.
Use a branching model rather than placing living species on a ladder from primitive to advanced.
trap: A modern organism is not inherently an unevolved version of another modern organism.
challenge: Why do closely related species often share more sequence similarity at a homologous locus?
solution: They often share a more recent common ancestor and have had less time for independent changes, although rates, selection and gene histories complicate simple comparisons.

questions.prompt: What does a branching tree represent?
options: Only the current body sizes of species.
Hypotheses about shared ancestry and divergence.
A ranking of moral value.
A guarantee that one living tip is the parent of another.
questions.explain: Hypotheses about shared ancestry and divergence.
questions.hint: A modern organism is not inherently an unevolved version of another modern organism.

questions.prompt: Why can conserved machinery support common ancestry?
options: Complex shared molecular features can be inherited from a shared ancestral system.
Every similarity must prove an identical recent ancestor.
Evolution predicts no similarities.
Only fossils can provide evidence.
questions.explain: Complex shared molecular features can be inherited from a shared ancestral system.
questions.hint: A modern organism is not inherently an unevolved version of another modern organism.

title: Recognize evolution as an ongoing population process
goal: Recognize evolution as an ongoing population process. Practice: design a temporal comparison.
idea: Evolution can be observed as inherited population changes across generations. Resistance, shifts in life-history traits and responses to altered environments can be studied with temporal data and experiments. Separate population change from an individual’s reversible response. Scientific conclusions should match measured inheritance and sampling evidence.
formula: Measure heritable variation across generations
steps: Measure resistance before and after several reproductive cycles under exposure.
Compare with unexposed control populations.
Test whether resistance persists in descendants under common conditions.
A persistent inherited shift supports evolution, whereas a temporary response in exposed individuals alone is insufficient.
trap: Evolution does not stop when a lineage appears well adapted.
challenge: How can common-environment testing help distinguish acclimation from inherited change?
solution: It reduces immediate environmental differences, allowing persistent descendant differences to be examined; additional genetic or inheritance evidence can refine the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which observation best supports an evolutionary change?
options: A heritable trait-frequency shift across generations.
A single leaf wilting and recovering within an hour.
One organism choosing a new location.
An unreplicated change in a detector setting.
questions.explain: A heritable trait-frequency shift across generations.
questions.hint: Evolution does not stop when a lineage appears well adapted.

questions.prompt: Why retain unexposed control populations?
options: To guarantee no mutations ever occur.
To force identical allele frequencies in every replicate.
To eliminate the need for replication.
To compare changes that occur without the experimental exposure.
questions.explain: To compare changes that occur without the experimental exposure.
questions.hint: Evolution does not stop when a lineage appears well adapted.

title: Read a phylogenetic tree by its branching pattern
goal: Read a phylogenetic tree by its branching pattern. Practice: analyze a visual representation.
idea: A tree’s topology represents relationships; rotating branches around a node does not change those relationships. A clade includes an ancestor and all its descendants. Time or amount of change is represented by branch length only when a scale or interpretation is explicitly given. Similar tip placement on a page is not a measure of relatedness.
formula: Most recent shared ancestor determines sister relationships
steps: A rooted topology places A and B together, with C branching earlier.
A and B share a more recent common ancestor with each other than with C.
Rotating the A-B node swaps their drawn positions without changing ancestry.
Do not infer that A evolved from living B or that an unscaled branch gives an exact date.
trap: Horizontal spacing or tip order alone does not establish relatedness.
challenge: A tree shows ((A,B),C). Is A more closely related to C than B is? Explain.
solution: No. A and B share the same relevant common ancestor with C in that topology. Their page positions do not create different relationships.

questions.prompt: What remains unchanged when a node’s branches are rotated?
options: The identity of the common ancestors is erased.
Every lineage becomes a direct ancestor of another tip.
Time runs backward.
The tree’s ancestry relationships.
questions.explain: The tree’s ancestry relationships.
questions.hint: Horizontal spacing or tip order alone does not establish relatedness.

questions.prompt: What defines a clade?
options: Only the living tip farthest to the right.
All organisms excluding an arbitrarily chosen descendant.
An ancestor and all descendants represented from it.
Any two species with similar color.
questions.explain: An ancestor and all descendants represented from it.
questions.hint: Horizontal spacing or tip order alone does not establish relatedness.

title: Explain reproductive isolation and speciation
goal: Explain reproductive isolation and speciation. Practice: explain a speciation model.
idea: Reduced gene flow can allow populations to diverge, while reproductive barriers limit successful interbreeding. Barriers can act before fertilization or after hybrid formation. Geographic isolation can promote divergence but does not alone guarantee a new species. Species concepts have different uses and limits, especially for asexual organisms and fossils.
formula: Reduced gene flow + divergence can produce reproductive isolation
steps: A geographic barrier separates a breeding population.
Mutation, drift and selection can change each population independently.
Later contact may reveal reduced mating or reduced hybrid fertility.
The barrier’s existence alone did not prove isolation; reproductive or other relevant evidence is needed.
trap: Speciation is not simply one individual moving to a new habitat.
challenge: Contrast a mating-time barrier with low hybrid fertility.
solution: Different mating times can prevent fertilization, a prezygotic barrier. Low hybrid fertility acts after a hybrid forms, a postzygotic barrier.

questions.prompt: Which is a prezygotic barrier?
options: Death of hybrid offspring after birth.
Reduced fertility of surviving hybrids.
Different mating seasons that prevent interbreeding.
Sterile hybrids after fertilization.
questions.explain: Different mating seasons that prevent interbreeding.
questions.hint: Speciation is not simply one individual moving to a new habitat.

questions.prompt: Why does geographic separation not guarantee speciation?
options: Gene flow always increases without contact.
Reproductive isolation may not develop, and populations can remain compatible.
Separated populations cannot mutate.
All individuals must become genetically identical.
questions.explain: Reproductive isolation may not develop, and populations can remain compatible.
questions.hint: Speciation is not simply one individual moving to a new habitat.

title: Distinguish the origin and maintenance of variation
goal: Distinguish the origin and maintenance of variation. Practice: analyze variation.
idea: Mutation introduces new sequence variants; recombination reshuffles existing alleles. Selection, drift and gene flow influence variation over time. Environmental dependence, heterozygote advantage or other balancing processes can maintain multiple alleles. Genetic variation is a population property, not proof that every variant is adaptive.
formula: New variants arise; population processes alter their frequencies
steps: Two alleles remain in a population where heterozygotes have the highest reproductive contribution under specified conditions.
Each homozygote is relatively disadvantaged in that model.
Selection can maintain both alleles rather than removing all but one.
The predicted outcome depends on fitness relationships and the rest of the population model.
trap: Natural selection can maintain variation; it does not always eliminate every alternative allele.
challenge: Why can a harmful allele persist?
solution: Its effects may be recessive, context dependent or offset by other fitness effects; mutation, migration and drift can also contribute. A specific case needs evidence.

questions.prompt: What directly introduces a new DNA sequence variant?
options: A membrane channel opening.
Mutation.
Independent assortment alone without any sequence change.
A stable genotype being translated twice.
questions.explain: Mutation.
questions.hint: Natural selection can maintain variation; it does not always eliminate every alternative allele.

questions.prompt: Which can maintain alleles through balancing selection?
options: Higher relative fitness of heterozygotes than either homozygote in the stated environment.
A requirement that all genotypes reproduce identically forever.
No reproduction in any genotype.
A guaranteed absence of mutation in every species.
questions.explain: Higher relative fitness of heterozygotes than either homozygote in the stated environment.
questions.hint: Natural selection can maintain variation; it does not always eliminate every alternative allele.

title: Evaluate testable models for early life
goal: Evaluate testable models for early life. Practice: evaluate limits of evidence.
idea: Origins-of-life research investigates plausible steps such as abiotic synthesis, compartment formation and self-replicating chemical systems. Early Earth differed from the modern oxygen-rich atmosphere. Laboratory plausibility does not prove that one exact historical pathway occurred. RNA can combine information storage with catalytic activity, motivating some hypotheses.
formula: A successful model demonstrates possibility, not a complete historical reconstruction
steps: A controlled experiment produces organic molecules from simpler inputs under selected conditions.
Identify what inputs and energy sources were supplied.
Compare with controls that omit key conditions.
The result supports chemical plausibility under those conditions, not the spontaneous appearance of a modern cell or proof of the unique historical route.
trap: Modern biological structures cannot be assumed to have appeared fully formed in one step.
challenge: Why are compartment-like structures relevant to early-life models?
solution: Boundaries can concentrate components and connect a chemical system’s properties to persistence and reproduction-like behavior, without alone demonstrating a living cell.

questions.prompt: What does abiotic synthesis in an experiment establish most directly?
options: Certain molecules can form under the tested nonliving conditions.
The exact historical origin of every organism is proven.
A modern cell was necessarily created.
No other pathway could have occurred.
questions.explain: Certain molecules can form under the tested nonliving conditions.
questions.hint: Modern biological structures cannot be assumed to have appeared fully formed in one step.

questions.prompt: Why is RNA relevant to some early-life hypotheses?
options: It contains no chemical bonds.
It cannot interact with other molecules.
It is always more stable than DNA under every condition.
It can carry sequence information and, in some forms, catalyze reactions.
questions.explain: It can carry sequence information and, in some forms, catalyze reactions.
questions.hint: Modern biological structures cannot be assumed to have appeared fully formed in one step.

title: Design experiments on responses to the environment
goal: Design experiments on responses to the environment. Practice: design an investigation.
idea: Organisms respond to cues through mechanisms shaped by evolution and development. Distinguish a behavioral or physiological response from an inherited population change. To test a cue, control alternatives such as temperature, moisture, chemical concentration and position effects, and use replication and appropriate randomization.
formula: A cue-response claim needs a controlled comparison
steps: Place organisms in a chamber with one shaded and one lit side.
Randomize which side receives shade across trials and monitor temperature.
Record locations after a predefined interval using independent replicates.
Greater shaded-side occupancy supports a light-associated response only to the extent that confounding variables are controlled.
trap: Movement toward one side does not identify its cause if several conditions differ together.
challenge: How would you test whether moisture rather than light explains a chamber preference?
solution: Manipulate moisture independently of light, ideally with a factorial design and replication, while controlling temperature and chamber position.

questions.prompt: What is an important control in a two-sided choice chamber?
options: Always put the treatment on the left.
Count only the first organism.
Change temperature and light together without measurement.
Counterbalance side assignments and control other environmental differences.
questions.explain: Counterbalance side assignments and control other environmental differences.
questions.hint: Movement toward one side does not identify its cause if several conditions differ together.

questions.prompt: A reversible response within an individual is automatically…
options: A change in population allele frequency.
Evidence that inheritance is absent.
Neither proof of inherited evolutionary change nor proof of a DNA mutation.
Proof of a new species.
questions.explain: Neither proof of inherited evolutionary change nor proof of a DNA mutation.
questions.hint: Movement toward one side does not identify its cause if several conditions differ together.

title: Track energy flow and matter cycling in ecosystems
goal: Track energy flow and matter cycling in ecosystems. Practice: track energy quantitatively.
idea: Energy enters most ecosystems through primary production and leaves transfers partly as heat. Matter is recycled through biological and environmental processes. Trophic transfer efficiencies vary, so a fixed percentage is a model assumption, not a universal constant. Net primary production is energy retained after producer respiration.
formula: NPP = GPP − producer respiration
steps: A simplified system has GPP=1200 energy units and producer respiration=500.
NPP is700 units available for producer growth and related transfers.
If a model assumes10% transfer to an herbivore level, that transfer is70 units.
The assumption does not mean all real ecosystems transfer exactly10%, and energy is not recycled like atoms.
trap: Energy flows through ecosystems; matter can cycle. Decomposers do not recycle used energy back into sunlight.
challenge: If GPP is900 and producer respiration350, calculate NPP and explain what the subtraction represents.
solution: NPP=550 units. Producer respiration uses part of the captured energy, leaving net stored production.

questions.prompt: For GPP=1000 and producer respiration=400, what is NPP?
questions.hint: Subtract producer respiration from gross production.
questions.explain: 1000−400=600 energy units in the stated interval.

questions.prompt: Why is energy usually lower at higher trophic levels?
options: Every ecosystem has exactly the same transfer percentage.
Transfers involve respiration, heat and material not consumed or assimilated.
Matter disappears completely at each transfer.
Consumers create energy from nothing.
questions.explain: Transfers involve respiration, heat and material not consumed or assimilated.
questions.hint: Energy flows through ecosystems; matter can cycle. Decomposers do not recycle used energy back into sunlight.

title: Model population growth with explicit assumptions
goal: Model population growth with explicit assumptions. Practice: interpret a population model.
idea: Population change reflects births, deaths, immigration and emigration. Exponential growth assumes a constant per-capita rate in a simplified setting. Logistic growth adds a density-related limitation through carrying capacity K. Real populations can fluctuate, experience delays and face changing environments.
formula: Exponential: dN/dt=rN; logistic: dN/dt=rN(1−N/K)
steps: A population has N=100,r=0.2 per time unit and K=500 in a logistic model.
Its instantaneous predicted change is0.2×100×(1−100/500)=16 individuals per time unit.
This is a rate at that state, not automatically the exact net change over a whole interval.
Compare measured time-series data with the model rather than assuming every population follows a smooth curve.
trap: Carrying capacity is not necessarily a fixed property of a species independent of its environment.
challenge: For N=200,r=0.1,K=400, calculate the logistic instantaneous growth rate.
solution: 0.1×200×(1−200/400)=10 individuals per time unit.

questions.prompt: For N=100,r=0.2,K=500, what is the logistic instantaneous growth rate?
questions.hint: Use rN(1−N/K).
questions.explain: 0.2×100×0.8=16 individuals per time unit.

questions.prompt: Which event directly adds individuals to a local population?
options: Immigration.
Emigration.
Death without replacement.
A decrease in resource supply by itself.
questions.explain: Immigration.
questions.hint: Carrying capacity is not necessarily a fixed property of a species independent of its environment.

title: Distinguish density dependence from density independence
goal: Distinguish density dependence from density independence. Practice: analyze density data.
idea: A density-dependent factor has effects that vary with population density, such as some forms of competition or disease transmission. Density-independent disturbances can act without their per-capita effect being determined by density. Real effects can interact, and a model’s K may shift as conditions change.
formula: Ask how per-capita effects change with density
steps: Maintain replicate populations at several starting densities with equal resource supply per container.
Measure per-capita growth over the same interval.
A decline in per-capita growth with density is consistent with density limitation.
Check alternative explanations such as waste accumulation or altered encounter rates rather than naming competition without evidence.
trap: A factor being severe does not make it density dependent; the relationship to density matters.
challenge: Why can adding food raise carrying capacity in one system but not another?
solution: Food may be limiting in the first system while another factor such as habitat space or water limits the second.

questions.prompt: Which observation supports density dependence?
options: Per-capita growth falls as density rises under controlled conditions.
A storm occurs once in a calendar year.
A population is large in one photograph.
Every individual has the same genotype.
questions.explain: Per-capita growth falls as density rises under controlled conditions.
questions.hint: A factor being severe does not make it density dependent; the relationship to density matters.

questions.prompt: What can change K in a logistic interpretation?
options: Only changing the species name.
Nothing; K is universally immutable.
A different axis color without a biological change.
A sustained change in limiting resources or environmental conditions.
questions.explain: A sustained change in limiting resources or environmental conditions.
questions.hint: A factor being severe does not make it density dependent; the relationship to density matters.

title: Analyze interactions and compare community data
goal: Analyze interactions and compare community data. Practice: analyze evidence and uncertainty.
idea: Competition, predation, herbivory, parasitism and mutualism affect interacting populations. Effects depend on context and can be indirect. Community comparisons require suitable sampling and uncertainty estimates. Error-bar interpretation depends on whether bars show variability, standard error or confidence intervals; overlap alone is not a universal significance test.
formula: Interaction effects can propagate through a community
steps: Exclude a predator from replicated plots while retaining matched control plots.
Measure herbivore abundance and plant biomass over time.
More herbivores and less plant biomass after exclusion are consistent with a trophic cascade.
Replication, initial comparability and other changes determine how strongly the experiment supports that causal interpretation.
trap: Correlation alone does not prove a direct interaction or exclude indirect causes.
challenge: A graph has overlapping standard-deviation bars. Can you automatically conclude no difference in means?
solution: No. Standard deviation describes spread, and overlap is not a universal test of mean differences. Identify the bars and use a suitable analysis and design.

questions.prompt: Which interaction benefits both partners under the stated conditions?
options: Competition by definition.
Predation by definition.
Parasitism by definition.
Mutualism.
questions.explain: Mutualism.
questions.hint: Correlation alone does not prove a direct interaction or exclude indirect causes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about error bars is most defensible?
options: No overlap proves the treatment mechanism uniquely.
Error bars make replication unnecessary.
Interpret them using their definition, sampling and analysis rather than overlap alone.
Any overlap proves the means identical.
questions.explain: Interpret them using their definition, sampling and analysis rather than overlap alone.
questions.hint: Correlation alone does not prove a direct interaction or exclude indirect causes.

title: Distinguish richness, evenness and ecological effects
goal: Distinguish richness, evenness and ecological effects. Practice: compare community representations.
idea: Biodiversity includes multiple levels, such as genetic, species and ecosystem variation. Species richness counts species; evenness describes their relative abundances. Communities with the same richness can differ strongly in composition and function. The effects of losing a species depend on its roles and the broader interaction network.
formula: Richness and relative abundance describe different properties
steps: Community A has four species with25 individuals each.
Community B has four species with97,1,1,1 individuals.
Both have richness4, but A is more even.
This comparison alone does not prove identical stability or productivity; those outcomes need separate evidence.
trap: More species does not automatically guarantee every possible measure of ecosystem function is higher.
challenge: Why can removal of a keystone species have a large effect despite low abundance?
solution: Its interactions can strongly organize the community, so abundance alone does not measure the magnitude of its ecological influence.

questions.prompt: A sample contains five distinct species with unequal abundances. What is its observed species richness?
questions.hint: Richness counts distinct species, not total individuals.
questions.explain: Five different species means observed richness5.

questions.prompt: Which comparison isolates evenness at equal richness?
options: Only comparing total leaf area.
Same number of species but different relative abundance distributions.
Different numbers of species with no abundance data only.
One sample measured without a count.
questions.explain: Same number of species but different relative abundance distributions.
questions.hint: More species does not automatically guarantee every possible measure of ecosystem function is higher.

title: Evaluate ecosystem disruptions and alternative explanations
goal: Evaluate ecosystem disruptions and alternative explanations. Practice: evaluate a hypothesis.
idea: Invasive species, habitat change, nutrient enrichment and climate-related shifts can alter communities. Effects can be indirect and depend on local conditions. A disruption can favor preexisting variants through selection, but does not direct specific adaptive mutations. Evaluate predictions using controlled or carefully designed observational evidence.
formula: Identify a perturbation, mechanism, evidence and uncertainty
steps: Extra nutrients enter a lake.
Increased primary production can supply more organic matter for decomposition.
Microbial respiration during decomposition can lower dissolved oxygen.
Oxygen loss is therefore compatible with nutrient-driven eutrophication, but temperature, flow and other factors should also be measured.
trap: More nutrient input does not always mean more oxygen available to every organism over time.
challenge: Why can a newly introduced species increase rapidly in one location but not another?
solution: Predators, competitors, resources, climate and reproductive opportunities differ. Introduction alone does not guarantee invasiveness.

questions.prompt: What can connect nutrient enrichment to oxygen depletion?
options: Only fish create all dissolved oxygen.

questions.explain: Decomposition-associated respiration consuming dissolved oxygen.
questions.hint: More nutrient input does not always mean more oxygen available to every organism over time.
